citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, in particular a finite Weyl reflection group, with $r=\dim V$. Put $S=\mathbb C[V]$, $R=S^W$, $I=SR_+$, and let $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ be the degrees of basic invariants. Then
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(S/I,t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{d_i-1}),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}(S/I)=\prod_i d_i=|W|.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. A **finite reduced crystallographic root system** is a finite subset $\Phi\subseteq E\setminus\{0\}$ spanning $E$, such that for every $\alpha,\beta\in\Phi$ the integer $\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2(\beta,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)$ is integral, the reflection $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ preserves $\Phi$, and the only scalar multiples of $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ are $\alpha,-\alpha$. The **Weyl group** $W$ is the subgroup of linear isometries of $E$ generated by these reflections. A **root reflection** means one of the $s_\alpha$. The empty root system on $E=0$ is allowed, with $W=\{1\}$.

Choose $t\in E$ such that $(t,\alpha)\ne0$ for every root. Put $\Phi^+=\{\alpha:(t,\alpha)>0\}$ and $\Phi^-=-\Phi^+$. A positive root is **simple** if it is not the sum of two positive roots. The following positive-root lemma proves that the simple roots form a basis $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and that the simple reflections $s_i=s_{\alpha_i}$ generate $W$; no such assertion is assumed by this definition. Once proved, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in a word for $w$ and let $\operatorname{Inv}(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi^+:w\alpha\in\Phi^-\}$. A word is reduced if its length equals $\ell(w)$.

Identify $E$ with its dual by the displayed form, so $\alpha^\vee=2\alpha/(\alpha,\alpha)$. The root and coroot groups are $Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha$ and $Q^\vee=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha^\vee$. The **weight group** is $P=\{\lambda\in E:(\lambda,\alpha^\vee)\in\mathbb Z\text{ for all }\alpha\in\Phi\}$; the positive-root lemma proves it is a lattice with basis the vectors dual to the simple coroots. Put $Q_+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$, and write $\mu\le\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q_+$. The open and closed positive chambers are $\mathcal C=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)>0\text{ for all }i\}$ and $\overline{\mathcal C}=\{x:(x,\alpha_i)\ge0\text{ for all }i\}$. A weight is dominant if it belongs to $P\cap\overline{\mathcal C}$. More generally chambers are the connected components of $E\setminus\bigcup_{\alpha\in\Phi}\alpha^\perp$. The closed-chamber representative and stabilizer assertions are proved later, not included as axioms.

Let $\Phi\subseteq E$ be a reduced crystallographic root system and let
$W=W(\Phi)$ be its Weyl group
([[def-weyl-group-of-a-root-system]]). Then $W$ acts simply transitively on
the set of open Weyl chambers of $\Phi$
([[def-open-and-closed-weyl-chambers]]): for any two open chambers $C,C'$
there is exactly one $w\in W$ with $w(C)=C'$.

Let $\Phi$ be the root system from [[thm-the-root-set-is-a-reduced-crystallographic-root-system]]. For a root $\alpha$, define the corresponding coroot by

$$\alpha^\vee:=\frac{2H_\alpha}{\alpha(H_\alpha)} \in \mathfrak h,$$

where $H_\alpha$ is the vector from [[def-killing-dual-vector-attached-to-a-root]]. The associated **root reflection** is the linear map

$$s_\alpha(\lambda):=\lambda-\lambda(\alpha^\vee)\alpha \qquad (\lambda\in \mathfrak h^*).$$

The subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(\mathfrak h^*)$ generated by these reflections is the **Weyl group** $W$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$ in the usual way.

derivations.claim: Molien trace identity: for $|t|<1$, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)=\sum_{d\ge0}\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^W)_dt^d=\frac1{|W|}\sum_{w\in W}\det(1-tw|_E)^{-1}.$$ Indeed the $W$-averaging operator $\pi=(1/|W|)\sum_ww$ is a projection onto $S^W$ in each finite-dimensional degree $S_d$, so $\dim(S^W)_d=\operatorname{tr}\pi|_{S_d}=(1/|W|)\sum_w\operatorname{tr}(w|_{S_d})$; on the other hand, for an operator with eigenvalues $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r$ on $E$, and hence $\mu_1^{-1},\dots,\mu_r^{-1}$ on $E^*$, the degree-$d$ trace $\operatorname{tr}(w|_{S_d})$ is the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial $h_d(\mu_1^{-1},\dots,\mu_r^{-1})$, whose generating function is $\prod_i(1-\mu_i^{-1}t)^{-1}=\det(1-tw^{-1}|_E)^{-1}$; averaging over $w$ and reindexing by $w\mapsto w^{-1}$ gives the displayed formula.

For $w\in W$ let $f$ be the dimension of its fixed space in $E$. Then $\det(1-tw|_E)=(1-t)^fg_w(t)$ with $g_w(t)=\prod_{\lambda
eq1}(1-t\lambda)$ over the remaining eigenvalues $\lambda$ of $w$ and $g_w(1)=\prod_{\lambda
eq1}(1-\lambda)
eq0$; all eigenvalues lie on the unit circle. In particular if $w
eq1$ fixes a hyperplane pointwise, then $f=r-1$, the remaining eigenvalue is $-1$, and $\det(1-tw|_E)=(1-t)^{r-1}(1+t)$.

If $w\in W$, $w
eq1$, fixes a hyperplane $H$ pointwise, then $H=\alpha^\perp$ for some root $\alpha$. A hyperplane is not the union of the finitely many proper closed subsets $H\cap eta^\perp$, so choose $x\in H$ with $(x, eta)
eq0$ for every root $ eta$; then $x$ lies in an open chamber $C$, and $w(x)=x$ gives $x\in C\cap w(C)$. As $w$ permutes the chambers, $C\cap w(C)
eq\varnothing$ forces $w(C)=C$, so $w$ lies in the stabilizer of $C$, which is trivial by simple transitivity. Hence $H$ is contained in a root hyperplane, and since both are hyperplanes, $H=\alpha^\perp$ for a root $\alpha$.

Put $u=1-t$. Since $1-t^{d_i}=1-(1-u)^{d_i}=d_iu-\frac{d_i(d_i-1)}2u^2+O(u^3)$, one has $(1-t^{d_i})^{-1}=d_i^{-1}u^{-1}(1+\frac{d_i-1}2u+O(u^2))$, and therefore $$\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{d_i})^{-1}=\Bigl(\prod_id_i\Bigr)^{-1}u^{-r}\Bigl(1+\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2u+O(u^2)\Bigr)=\frac1{|W|}u^{-r}\Bigl(1+\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2u+O(u^2)\Bigr),$$ the last equality by [F1]; this product equals $\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)$ for $|t|<1$ by [F1].

The map $\alpha\mapsto s_\alpha$ induces a bijection from the set $\Phi^+$ of positive roots onto the set of reflections in $W$; consequently $W$ has exactly $|\Phi^+|$ reflections. Injectivity: $s_\alpha=s_\beta$ forces the two reflections to have the same fixed hyperplane, so $\beta=\pm\alpha$, and among positive roots $\beta=\alpha$. Surjectivity: every reflection of $W$ has a fixed hyperplane, which is $\alpha^\perp$ for some root $\alpha$ by step 1.3, and the reflection of $E$ with fixed hyperplane $\alpha^\perp$ is unique, namely $s_\alpha$. Since $s_\alpha=s_{-\alpha}$ and every root hyperplane is $\alpha^\perp$ for exactly one positive root by [F3], distinct positive roots give distinct reflections.

Expanding the right-hand side of step 1.1 at $t=1$ in the variable $u=1-t$ gives $$\frac1{|W|}\sum_{w\in W}\det(1-tw|_E)^{-1}=\frac1{|W|}\Bigl(u^{-r}+\frac{|\Phi^+|}2u^{-(r-1)}+O(u^{-(r-2)})\Bigr).$$ The identity $w=1$ contributes $u^{-r}$. A nonidentity $w$ with fixed space of dimension $r-1$ is a reflection, and there are exactly $|\Phi^+|$ of them by step 2.1; each contributes $\det(1-tw)^{-1}=(1-t)^{-(r-1)}(1+t)^{-1}=u^{-(r-1)}(\frac12+O(u))$ by step 1.2, because $(1+t)^{-1}=(2-u)^{-1}=\frac12+O(u)$. Every other nonidentity $w$ has $f\le r-2$, hence contributes $u^{-f}\cdot O(1)=O(u^{-(r-2)})$ by step 1.2.

Steps 1.4 and 3.1 compute the same meromorphic function of $u$ near $u=0$; comparing the coefficients of $u^{-(r-1)}$, which are finite, gives $\frac1{|W|}\cdot\frac{\sum_i(d_i-1)}2=\frac1{|W|}\cdot\frac{|\Phi^+|}2$, hence $\sum_i(d_i-1)=|\Phi^+|$.

With the page degree normalization $\deg E=2$ the basic invariant $w_i$ has page degree $2d_i$, so the coinvariant algebra has Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})/(1-t^2)^r$ and its top degree is $\sum_i2d_i-2r=2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2|\Phi^+|=|\Phi|$, by step 4.1 and the published degree computation for the coinvariant algebra.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, set $S=S(\mathfrak g)$, $R=S^{\mathfrak g}$, and let $\mathcal H$ be its Kostant harmonic subspace. Multiplication is an isomorphism
$$R\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S$$
of graded $\mathfrak g$-modules, where $R$ carries the trivial action. The assertion includes $\mathfrak g=0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra, let
$\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$ be any Cartan subalgebra in the nilpotent self-normalizing sense, and let $W$ be its
Weyl group. Restriction to $\mathfrak h$ induces an algebra isomorphism

$$S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g} \xrightarrow{\sim} S(\mathfrak h)^W.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, in particular a finite Weyl reflection group, with $r=\dim V$. Put $S=\mathbb C[V]$, $R=S^W$, $I=SR_+$, and let $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ be the degrees of basic invariants. Then
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(S/I,t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{d_i-1}),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}(S/I)=\prod_i d_i=|W|.$$

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Fix the finite Weyl root-system data of
[[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]: the real span
$E$ of the roots with its positive definite form, a positive system $\Phi^+$
with base $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$, the root group
$Q=\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathbb Z\alpha\subseteq P$, the weight lattice
$P\subseteq E$, and the positive cone
$$Q_+=\sum_{i=1}^r\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$$
(the set written $Q^+$ in
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]]). A **downward cone**
is a set $\lambda-Q_+=\{\lambda-\beta:\beta\in Q_+\}$ with
$\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$.

The **completed formal character ring** $\mathcal R$ is the set of formal sums
$$f=\sum_{\mu\in\mathfrak h^*}c_\mu e^\mu,\qquad c_\mu\in\mathbb Z,$$
whose support $\operatorname{supp}f=\{\mu:c_\mu\ne0\}$ is contained in a
finite union of downward cones. Addition is coefficientwise, the product is
the convolution
$$(fg)_\eta=\sum_{\mu+\nu=\eta}c_\mu d_\nu,$$
and the unit is $e^0$, so that $e^\mu e^\nu=e^{\mu+\nu}$. The product is
well defined: if $\operatorname{supp}f$ lies in
$\bigcup_{i=1}^m(\lambda_i-Q_+)$ and $\operatorname{supp}g$ in
$\bigcup_{j=1}^n(\mu_j-Q_+)$, then a pair of exponents contributing to $\eta$
lies in some $\lambda_i-Q_+$ and some $\mu_j-Q_+$, and the solutions
$\beta,\gamma\in Q_+$ of $\beta+\gamma=\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta$ are the elements
of the box $0\le\beta_k\le(\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta)_k$ in the simple-root
coordinates, a finite set (empty unless $\lambda_i+\mu_j-\eta\in Q_+$). The
coefficients are integers, and a finite union of downward cones is again such
a union, so addition and multiplication make $\mathcal R$ a commutative
$\mathbb Z$-algebra. In the notation of
[[def-grothendieck-group-and-character-of-category-o]] this is the ring
denoted $\mathscr R$ there, where the character homomorphism of category
$\mathcal O$ takes its values; the elements of finite support form the group
ring $\mathbb Z[\mathfrak h^*]$ of the additive group $\mathfrak h^*$ and
contain the subring $\mathbb Z[P]$ generated by the $e^\mu$ with
$\mu\in P$.

By [[prop-formal-character-of-a-verma-module]],
$$\operatorname{ch}M(\lambda)=e^\lambda\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$$
is an element of $\mathcal R$: the geometric series
$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-k\alpha}$ is supported in the downward cone $-Q_+$, and a
finite product of elements of $\mathcal R$ lies in $\mathcal R$ by the
convolution formula, while $e^\lambda$ is a single monomial. **No convergence
of any formal sum is asserted**: all sums are formal, coefficients are
compared coefficientwise, and every finite sum, product or finite product of
geometric series below is interpreted in $\mathcal R$ by the rules just
recorded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). For every dominant
integral weight $\lambda\in\Lambda^+$, the character of the finite-dimensional
simple module $L(\lambda)$ is
$$\operatorname{ch}L(\lambda)=A(\lambda+\rho)\cdot A(\rho)^{-1}=\Bigl(\sum_{w\in W}(-1)^{\ell(w)}e^{w(\lambda+\rho)}\Bigr)\Big/\Bigl(e^{\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})\Bigr),$$
the quotient being taken in the completed character ring $\mathcal R$ of
[[def-completed-formal-character-ring-for-downward-cones]], where
$A(\rho)$ is invertible with inverse
$e^{-\rho}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}$
([[thm-weyl-denominator-identity]],
[[lem-geometric-series-invertibility-in-the-completed-character-ring]]). No
quotient of ordinary functions is intended before this formal cancellation is
justified.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, the enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak g)$ is a free left, hence also right, module over its center $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

derivations.claim: Write $C=S/(R_+S)$ for the coinvariant algebra of the adjoint action. By [F1], $S_d=(R_+S)_d\oplus\mathcal H_d$ in every degree, with both summands $\mathfrak g$-stable; hence the quotient map restricts to an isomorphism $\mathcal H\to C$ of graded $\mathfrak g$-modules, and each $\mathcal H_d$ is finite dimensional. In particular the multiplicity series $H_E(q):=\sum_{d\ge0}\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)q^d$ has nonnegative integer coefficients.

By [F2] the ring $R$ is a polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[p_1,\dots,p_r]$ on homogeneous generators $p_i$ of degrees $d_i$, and the Hilbert series $\operatorname{Hilb}(R,q)=\prod_i(1-q^{d_i})^{-1}$ arises from the graded algebra structure of $R$ on $S$. Also $\prod_id_i=|W|$.

Since $R$ acts on $S$ by $R$-linear maps commuting with $\mathfrak g$ and acts trivially on $E$, evaluating on $E$ gives an isomorphism of graded $R$-modules $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\cong R\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$. Indeed $R\otimes\mathcal H$ is free over $R$ on $\mathcal H$ and the adjoint action is $R$-linear, so $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(E,R\otimes\mathcal H)\cong R\otimes\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(E,\mathcal H)$ as $R$-modules and taking $\mathfrak g$-invariants commutes with the graded direct sum. Consequently $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)$ is a free graded $R$-module exactly when $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$ is finite dimensional, and then its rank is $\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)=H_E(1)$.

The graded character of $S$ is $\operatorname{ch}S=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-qe^{\alpha})^{-1}\cdot(1-q)^{-r}$: the weights of $\mathfrak g$ under the adjoint action are the roots $\alpha\in\Phi$ together with $0$ with multiplicity $r$, and the symmetric algebra on a finite-dimensional module with weights $\mu$ has character $\prod_\mu(1-qe^\mu)^{-1}$ in the completed character ring, the geometric series being invertible there.

The simple characters are orthonormal for the constant-term form $$\langle\phi,\psi\rangle=\frac1{|W|}\operatorname{CT}\bigl(\phi\,\psi^{*}\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-e^{\alpha})\bigr),\qquad \psi^{*}=\sum_\mu(\dim \psi_\mu)e^{-\mu},$$ where $\operatorname{CT}$ takes the coefficient of $e^0$: by [F4], $\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-e^{\alpha})=A(\rho)A(\rho)^{*}$, so the pairing of $\chi_E$ and $\chi_F$ equals $\frac1{|W|}\operatorname{CT}(A(E+\rho)A(F+\rho)^{*})$, and the constant term selects the pairs with $w(E+\rho)=w'(F+\rho)$; each dominant orbit has exactly $|W|$ terms and the signs multiply to $1$, so the value is $\delta_{EF}$.

Realize constant terms as matrix coefficients on $\ell^2(P)$, $P$ the weight lattice, with orthonormal basis $\delta_\mu$: for a root $\alpha$ put $U_\alpha\delta_\mu=\delta_{\mu-\alpha}$, so multiplication by $e^{\alpha}$ corresponds to $U_\alpha$. For $0\le q<1$ the operators $F_\alpha(q)=(I-U_\alpha)(I-qU_\alpha)^{-1}$ are bounded and commute, and $F_{-\alpha}(q)=F_\alpha(q)^{*}$; hence $T(q)=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}F_\alpha(q)=\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}F_\alpha(q)F_\alpha(q)^{*}$ is self-adjoint, and $\|F_\alpha(q)\|\le 2$ for $q\ge\frac12$ because a spectral value $\lambda$ of $U_\alpha$ lies on the unit circle and $|1-\lambda|^2\le q^{-1}|1-q\lambda|^2$. Moreover $(F_\alpha(q)-I)\delta_0=-(1-q)\sum_{n\ge0}q^n\delta_{(n+1)\alpha}$ has squared norm $\frac{1-q}{1+q}\to0$, so expanding $\prod_\alpha F_\alpha(q)-I$ as a telescoping sum with one factor $F_\alpha(q)-I$ per term and all other factors bounded by $2$ gives $\|T(q)\delta_0-\delta_0\|\to0$ as $q\to1^{-}$.

By [F3] each finite-dimensional $\mathcal H_d$ decomposes into isotypic components, so $\operatorname{ch}\mathcal H=\sum_E H_E(q)\chi_E$ in the completed character ring, the sum over isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-modules; both sides are formal power series whose coefficients are finite characters.

Since $R$ has trivial $\mathfrak g$-action, the decomposition $S=R\otimes\mathcal H$ of [F1] tensors characters: $\operatorname{ch}S=\operatorname{Hilb}(R,q)\cdot\operatorname{ch}\mathcal H$. Combining with steps 1.2, 1.4 and 1.7, $$\operatorname{ch}\mathcal H=\prod_i[d_i]_q\cdot\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}(1-qe^{\alpha})^{-1},\qquad [d_i]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{d_i-1}.$$

Interpreting a finitely supported character as the finite combination of shifts $\psi\mapsto\sum_\mu\psi_\mu U_{-\mu}$ identifies the constant term of step 1.6 with a matrix coefficient: $$\operatorname{CT}\Bigl(\psi\prod_{\alpha\in\Phi}\frac{1-e^{\alpha}}{1-qe^{\alpha}}\Bigr)=\langle\psi\,T(q)\delta_0,\delta_0\rangle.$$

Applying the orthonormality of step 1.5 to the expansion 2.1 gives, for each finite-dimensional simple $E$, with $\chi_E^{*}$ as in step 1.5 and the matrix-coefficient form of step 2.2, $$H_E(q)=\prod_i[d_i]_q\cdot\frac1{|W|}\langle\chi_E^{*}T(q)\delta_0,\delta_0\rangle.$$ This is an identity of formal power series in $q$ with rational coefficients.

Letting $q\to1^{-}$ in step 3.1, the matrix coefficient tends to $\langle\chi_E^{*}\delta_0,\delta_0\rangle=\dim E_0$ by the second part of step 1.6, and $\prod_i[d_i]_q\to\prod_id_i=|W|$ by step 1.2; hence $\lim_{q\to1^{-}}H_E(q)=\dim E_0$.

The coefficients $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)$ of $H_E(q)$ are nonnegative integers and $H_E(q)$ is increasing for $0\le q<1$; the finite limit $\dim E_0$ of step 4.1 therefore forces $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)=0$ for all but finitely many $d$ and $\sum_d\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H_d)=\dim E_0$. Hence $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$ is finite dimensional of dimension $\dim E_0$, and by step 1.3 the module $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)$ is a finitely generated graded free $R$-module of rank $\dim E_0$.

The identification of step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,C)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$ as graded vector spaces, so $\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,C)=\dim E_0$; tensoring the isomorphism of step 1.3 with $C$ over $R$ and using $S\otimes_RC=C$ shows that $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\otimes_RC\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,C)$ is an isomorphism. This is the asserted compatibility with the natural quotient map $S\to C=S/(R_+S)$.

By [F5] the symmetrization $\operatorname{sym}$ is filtered, $\mathfrak g$-equivariant with associated graded the identity, and the symmetrized lifts of a homogeneous basis of $\mathcal H$ form a $Z$-basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$; thus $U(\mathfrak g)=Z\cdot\operatorname{sym}(\mathcal H)\cong Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{sym}(\mathcal H)$ with $Z$ acting trivially under the adjoint action. Applying the argument of step 1.3 with $Z$ in place of $R$ and $\operatorname{sym}(\mathcal H)$ in place of $\mathcal H$ gives an isomorphism of $Z$-modules $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,U(\mathfrak g))\cong Z\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$; by step 5.1 this is a free $Z$-module of rank $\dim E_0$.

For every central character with kernel $\mathfrak m\subseteq Z$ the reduction satisfies $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,U(\mathfrak g)\otimes_ZZ/\mathfrak m)\cong(Z/\mathfrak m)\otimes_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,\mathcal H)$, of dimension $\dim E_0$ over $Z/\mathfrak m$; in the polynomial family the reductions $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,S)\otimes_RR/\mathfrak m$ have the same rank $\dim E_0$, and the special case $R/\mathfrak m=C$ is step 6.1. Hence every central reduction has adjoint $E$-multiplicity $\dim E_0$.

For later use we record that the argument also applies to a finite direct sum: if $E=\bigoplus_jE_j$ is a finite direct sum of finite-dimensional modules, then $E_0=\bigoplus_j(E_j)_0$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E,-)\cong\bigoplus_j\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathfrak g}(E_j,-)$, so all ranks add and the conclusions hold with $\dim E_0=\sum_j\dim(E_j)_0$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from [F1], [F2] and [F5], namely from the Kostant decomposition, the Chevalley restriction and the free-over-center theorem; the multiplicity computation itself uses only finite-dimensional linear algebra, finite sums over the finite Weyl group and single root-lattice shifts.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with
Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and Weyl group $W$, acting on $\mathfrak h^*$
by the root reflections of [[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]]), hence on the
symmetric algebra $S=S(\mathfrak h^*)$ by graded algebra automorphisms; the
dual action identifies $S$ with $S(\mathfrak h)$ as a graded $W$-algebra, and
the page writes $S=S(\mathfrak h)$ for either. Write
$$S^W_+=\bigoplus_{d>0}(S^W)_d,\qquad I:=S\,S^W_+,$$
so that $I$ is the homogeneous ideal of $S$ generated by the invariants of
positive degree; this is the specialization to the reflection group case of
the quotient construction of
[[def-finite-linear-invariant-and-coinvariant-polynomial-algebras]], because
$S^W_+$ is exactly the space of positive-degree elements of the invariant
algebra $S^W$.

The **coinvariant algebra** of the pair $(\mathfrak h,W)$ is the graded
quotient
$$C=C(\mathfrak h,W):=S/I.$$
It is a commutative graded $\mathbb C$-algebra with $C_0=\mathbb C$: the ideal
$I$ is homogeneous of positive degree, so constants survive and every
homogeneous piece of $S$ maps onto its image. The quotient map
$$\rho:S\longrightarrow C,\qquad \rho(f)=f+I,$$
is a surjective graded algebra homomorphism, and the action of $W$ on $S$
descends to a $\mathbb C$-linear action on $C$ by graded algebra
automorphisms, because $I$ is $W$-stable. The algebra $C$ is finite
dimensional: $W$ is generated by its root reflections, so
[[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]] writes $S$ as a free
module of finite rank over the polynomial algebra $S^W$, and
[[lem-weyl-coinvariant-hilbert-series-has-order-w-dimension]] gives
$\dim_{\mathbb C}C=|W|<\infty$ with the graded Hilbert series recorded there.

**Degree normalization.** Throughout the Soergel material on this page the
Cartan generators are given degree $2$, that is $\deg\mathfrak h=2$; the
symmetric algebra $S$ is then graded with $\deg S_d=2d$ for homogeneous
polynomials of ordinary degree $d$, and $C$ inherits this doubled grading. In
particular a basic invariant of ordinary degree $d_i$ has page degree $2d_i$,
and the top nonzero degree of $C$ is $2N$ with
$N=\sum_i(d_i-1)$ the number of positive roots.

**Auxiliary permutation model for type $A$.** For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sl}_n$
one may instead work with the place-permuting $S_n$-action on the auxiliary
polynomial ring $S_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$, where a
permutation $\sigma$ sends $x_i$ to $x_{\sigma(i)}$, and with the quotient
$$C_{\mathrm{perm}}:=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
where $e_1,\dots,e_n$ are the elementary symmetric polynomials. Splitting the
permutation representation $\mathbb C^n=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathbb C\cdot(1,\dots,1)$
into its sum-zero Cartan part and its fixed average coordinate exhibits
$\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]\cong S(\mathfrak h)\otimes\mathbb C[e_1]$ with
$e_1=x_1+\cdots+x_n$ the invariant coordinate, and restriction to the hyperplane
$e_1=0$ has kernel $(e_1)$. Since $e_1,\dots,e_n$ generate the positive-degree
invariants of the permutation action, while $e_2,\dots,e_n$ restrict to basic
invariants of $S(\mathfrak h)^W$, dividing out by the positive-degree invariants
commutes with this presentation and yields a canonical isomorphism of graded
algebras
$$C(\mathfrak h,W)\cong C_{\mathrm{perm}}=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(e_1,\dots,e_n),$$
in which $x_i$ has degree $2$ and $e_i$ has degree $2i$. Elements of $C$ are
written as classes $\rho(f)$; the auxiliary model is used only for explicit
rank computations and never replaces the intrinsic definition.

All constructions above use only the finite Weyl group, its finite-dimensional
reflection representation and finite coordinate choices; no choice principle is
used.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, $n=\dim V$, $S=\mathbb C[V]$, and $R=S^G$. Let $f_1,\ldots,f_m$ be minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I=SR_+$, with $d_i=\deg f_i>0$. Their common zero set is $\{0\}$, $m=n$, and they form an $S$-regular sequence. Every homogeneous lift of a homogeneous complex basis of $S/I$ is a graded free $R$-basis of $S$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a finite ordered sequence in $R$, and let $M$ be an $R$-module. On $\bigwedge R^n$, with standard basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$, let $\delta$ be the $R$-linear graded derivation of degree $-1$ with $\delta(e_i)=x_i$ and $\delta(R)=0$; thus $\delta(ab)=\delta(a)b+(-1)^pa\delta(b)$ for homogeneous $a$ of degree $p$.

The **Koszul complex with coefficients in $M$** is $K(\mathbf x;M)=(\bigwedge R^n\otimes_R M,d)$, where $d=\delta\otimes\operatorname{id}_M$. Its degree-$p$ term is $\bigwedge^pR^n\otimes_R M$ for $0\leq p\leq n$, and zero otherwise. Explicitly,

$$d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes m)=\sum_{j=1}^p(-1)^{j-1}e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_j}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes x_{i_j}m.$$

The empty wedge is $1\in R$. In particular $d(e_i\otimes m)=1\otimes x_im$ in $K_0=R\otimes_R M$, canonically identified with $M$ by $r\otimes m\mapsto rm$ with inverse $m\mapsto1\otimes m$. The differential out of degree zero is zero. The derivation respects the exterior relations and the two orders of deleting distinct factors cancel in $d^2$, so these maps form a chain complex. For $n=0$ this is $M$ in degree zero under the same identification.
For a finite sequence $\mathbf x$, $H_0(K(\mathbf x;M))=M/(\mathbf x)M$, $H_i=0$ for $i>n$, and $H_n=\{m\in M:x_im=0\text{ for all }i\}$.
If $M$ is finite free and $\mathbf x$ is $M$-regular, then $K(\mathbf x;M)$ is a finite free resolution of $M/(\mathbf x)M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, in particular a finite Weyl reflection group, with $r=\dim V$. Put $S=\mathbb C[V]$, $R=S^W$, $I=SR_+$, and let $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ be the degrees of basic invariants. Then
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(S/I,t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{d_i-1}),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}(S/I)=\prod_i d_i=|W|.$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. Define polynomial rings in finitely many commuting indeterminates recursively by

$$ R[x_1,\ldots,x_0]:=R,\qquad R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n+1}]:=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n][x_{n+1}]. $$

At each stage the coefficient ring embeds as the constant polynomials ([[thm-polynomial-ring-is-a-commutative-ring]]), so all preceding indeterminates remain present. The new indeterminate commutes with every coefficient by the commutativity built into [[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]], and consequently all $x_i$ commute. This iterated ring is denoted $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$.

For a right $R$-module $N$ and a left $R$-module $M$ with a specified
projective resolution $P_\bullet\twoheadrightarrow M$, define the
left-resolution construction
$$\operatorname{Tor}^{R,P}_n(N,M):=H_n(N\otimes_RP_\bullet).$$
The datum $P$ remains in the notation until the balance and
change-of-resolution results prove that it may be suppressed.

For a right $R$-module $N$ with a specified projective resolution
$Q_\bullet\twoheadrightarrow N$ and a left $R$-module $M$, define the
right-resolution construction
$$\operatorname{Tor}^{R,Q}_n(N,M):=H_n(Q_\bullet\otimes_RM).$$
The datum $Q$ remains in the notation until the balance and change-of-resolution
results prove that it may be suppressed.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). For every right $R$-module $N$ and left
$R$-module $M$ with supplied projective resolutions $Q_\bullet\to N$ and
$P_\bullet\to M$, there is a natural isomorphism
$H_i(N\otimes_RP_\bullet)\cong H_i(Q_\bullet\otimes_RM)$.

derivations.claim: The invariant ideal is generated by the basic invariants: $I=S\,S^W_+=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, because $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ and every element of $S^W_+$ is a polynomial in the $w_i$ with zero constant term. Hence $C=S/(w_1,\dots,w_r)$; since $C$ is generated by the images of the degree-two elements, its augmentation ideal satisfies $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$.

The $r$ basic invariants form an $S$-regular sequence: they are minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ (they generate $I$, and no $w_i$ lies in the ideal generated by the others, since the $w_i$ are algebraically independent and all of positive degree), and by [F2] the minimal homogeneous invariant generators of $I$ are $r$ in number with common zero set $\{0\}$ and form an $S$-regular sequence; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf w;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $C$.
The variables $x_1,\dots,x_r$ form an $S$-regular sequence with $S/(x_1,\dots,x_r)=\mathbb C=:k$, by [F5]; consequently, by [F3], $K(\mathbf x;S)$ is a finite free resolution of $k$.

Koszul differentials vanish after base change to $k$: tensoring $K(\mathbf w;S)$ with $k$ multiplies by the images of the $w_i$ in $k$, which lie in the positive-degree part and hence act as zero; so $H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)=K_r(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk$, a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$.

First computation: by resolution 1.2 and the left-resolution construction of Tor, $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(K(\mathbf w;S)\otimes_Sk)$, which by step 1.4 is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$.

Second computation: by resolution 1.3 and the right-resolution construction of Tor, $\operatorname{Tor}^S_r(C,k)\cong H_r(C\otimes_SK(\mathbf x;S))=H_r(K(\mathbf x;C))$; by [F3] the top homology is $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$, placed in internal degree $2r$ above the degrees of its elements, since $e_1\wedge\cdots\wedge e_r$ carries degree $2r$.

Hilbert series: applying the Euler characteristic to the finite free resolution $K(\mathbf w;S)$ of $C$ gives $$\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\frac{\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})}{(1-t^2)^r}=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)}),$$ the last equality by cancelling one factor $1-t^2$ per invariant. Hence $\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ is a polynomial of degree $2N$ with leading coefficient $1$, so $\dim_{\mathbb C}C_{2N}=1$ and $C_j=0$ for $j>2N$; the classical formula [F4] gives the same series after substituting $t^2$ for $t$.

Comparing steps 2.1 and 2.2 through the natural isomorphism [F6] identifies the top Koszul homology of step 2.2 with a one-dimensional space in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i$; shifting back by the degree $2r$ of the top exterior generator, the space $\{c\in C:x_ic=0\text{ for all }i\}$ is one dimensional and concentrated in internal degree $\sum_i2d_i-2r=2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2N$.

Since $C_+=(x_1,\dots,x_r)C$ by step 1.1, the space of step 3.1 is exactly the socle $\operatorname{soc}(C)=\{c\in C:C_+c=0\}$; it is one dimensional in degree $2N$. The top graded piece $C_{2N}$ is one dimensional by step 2.3, and every element of $C_{2N}$ is annihilated by $C_+$ because $C$ has no degrees above $2N$; hence $0\neq C_{2N}\subseteq\operatorname{soc}(C)$ and both are one dimensional in degree $2N$, so $\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$.

Nondegeneracy of the top pairing: let $0
eq c\in C_i$ be homogeneous and consider the nonzero graded ideal $cC$ of the finite-dimensional graded algebra $C$; let $m$ be the largest degree with $(cC)_m
eq0$, so $m\le2N$ by step 2.3. Choose $0
eq y\in(cC)_m$; then $C_+y\subseteq(cC)_{>m}=0$, so $y\in\operatorname{soc}(C)=C_{2N}$ by step 4.1, forcing $m=2N$. Writing $y=cb$ with $b\in C_{2N-i}$ gives a nonzero product $cb$, so the pairing $C_i	imes C_{2N-i}	o C_{2N}\cong\mathbb C$ has no nonzero left radical; by commutativity it has no nonzero right radical either, and finite-dimensionality of the two sides makes it a perfect pairing for every $i$. Hence $C$ is a graded Gorenstein algebra with one-dimensional socle in top degree $2N$.

derivations.claim: Choose an arbitrary positive definite symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ and average it over the finite group $W$, obtaining a $W$-invariant positive definite form $(\ ,\ )$; choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ for it. On the symmetric algebra $S=\mathbb C[e_1,\dots,e_r]$ let $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ be the Fischer pairing, the sesquilinear form with $\langle e^{\alpha},e^{\beta}\rangle=\alpha!\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ on monomials $e^{\alpha}$ ($\alpha$ a multi-index); it is positive definite, and $W$ acts on $S$ by orthogonal transformations for it because the form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is $W$-invariant. For $p\in S$ let $\partial_p=p(\partial_1,\dots,\partial_r)$ be substitution of the partial derivatives $\partial_i=\partial/\partial e_i$; then multiplication by $p$ has adjoint $\partial_p$, i.e. $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_pg\rangle$, as checked on monomials. Set $\mathcal H_d:=I_d^{\perp}$ inside the finite-dimensional space $S_d$, and $\mathcal H:=\bigoplus_d\mathcal H_d$.

The invariant ring acts on $S$ with the expected Hilbert series: $S$ has a finite homogeneous $S^W$-basis by [F1], say of degrees $m_1,\dots,m_{|W|}$; their images in $S/S^W_+S=C$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis by graded Nakayama, so $\sum_jt^{m_j}=\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ and therefore $\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$.

By step 1.1 the spaces $S_d=I_d\oplus\mathcal H_d$ are orthogonal direct sums and $\mathcal H$ is a graded subspace; it is $W$-stable because $W$ preserves the form and $I$ is a $W$-stable homogeneous ideal, and $\mathcal H$ is a graded complement of $I$. Moreover $\mathcal H_d=\{f\in S_d:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\}$: since $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, one has $f\in I_d^{\perp}$ exactly when $\langle f,w_ig\rangle=0$ for every $i$ and every $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$, which by adjointness is $\langle\partial_{w_i}f,g\rangle=0$ for all such $g$, hence $\partial_{w_i}f=0$ by positive definiteness; and for $p=\sum_iq_iw_i$ one has $\partial_p=\sum_iq_i\partial_{w_i}$, so vanishing for the $w_i$ is vanishing for all of $S^W_+$.

The restriction $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\to C$ is an isomorphism of graded vector spaces because $\rho$ has kernel $I$ and $\mathcal H$ is a complement of $I$ by step 1.1; it is a map of $W$-modules because $\rho$ is $W$-equivariant. Hence $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$, and $\dim\mathcal H=\dim C=|W|$ by [F2].

Let $\varphi:S^W\otimes\mathcal H\to S$, $p\otimes h\mapsto ph$. This is a homomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules. Its reduction modulo $S^W_+$, namely $C\otimes\mathcal H\to C$, $c\otimes h\mapsto c\,\rho(h)$, is surjective because it restricts on $1\otimes\mathcal H$ to the isomorphism $\rho|_{\mathcal H}$ of step 2.2.

The map $\varphi$ is surjective: given homogeneous $f\in S_d$, choose $h\in\mathcal H_d$ with $\rho(f)=\rho(h)$ by step 3.1; then $f-h\in I_d=\sum_i(w_iS)_d=\sum_iw_iS_{d-2d_i}$, so by induction on $d$ each $w_ig$ with $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$ lies in $S^W\cdot\mathcal H$, and adding $h$ exhibits $f$ in the image.

The map $\varphi$ is injective: by steps 1.2 and 2.2 the two sides have the same Hilbert series, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W\otimes\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t),$$ both are graded with finite-dimensional graded pieces, and by step 4.1 the kernel of the surjective graded $S^W$-linear map $\varphi$ would otherwise contribute positive Hilbert series. Hence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.

Steps 2.1, 2.2 and 5.1 give a $W$-stable graded complement $\mathcal H$ of $I$ with $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\cong C$ and $S^W\otimes\mathcal H\cong S$; the description of $\mathcal H$ as the kernel of the Laplacian follows from the adjointness $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_pg\rangle$ of step 1.1, and $\dim\mathcal H=|W|$ by step 2.2. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory suppliers [F1] and [F2]; the construction itself uses only finite averages and finite-dimensional linear algebra.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, set $S=S(\mathfrak g)$, $R=S^{\mathfrak g}$, and let $\mathcal H$ be its Kostant harmonic subspace. Multiplication is an isomorphism
$$R\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S$$
of graded $\mathfrak g$-modules, where $R$ carries the trivial action. The assertion includes $\mathfrak g=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra, let
$\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathfrak g$ be any Cartan subalgebra in the nilpotent self-normalizing sense, and let $W$ be its
Weyl group. Restriction to $\mathfrak h$ induces an algebra isomorphism

$$S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g} \xrightarrow{\sim} S(\mathfrak h)^W.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from invariant theory. Let $\Phi$ be a
finite reduced crystallographic root system of rank $r$ in the real Cartan
space $E$ with Weyl group $W$
([[def-finite-weyl-root-system-lattice-and-chamber-conventions]],
[[def-root-reflections-and-the-weyl-group-action]]), and let
$S=\mathbb C[E]$ carry the induced graded $W$-action with Cartan generators in
ordinary degree $1$. Let $d_1,\dots,d_r$ be the ordinary degrees of basic
invariants, so that $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ with $w_i$ homogeneous of
degree $d_i$ ([[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]]). Then
$$\sum_{i=1}^r(d_i-1)=|\Phi^+|.$$
With the page degree normalization $\deg E=2$ the coinvariant algebra
$S/(S^W_+S)$ has top degree $2\sum_i(d_i-1)=2|\Phi^+|=|\Phi|$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, let $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ be a finite ordered sequence in $R$, and let $M$ be an $R$-module. On $\bigwedge R^n$, with standard basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$, let $\delta$ be the $R$-linear graded derivation of degree $-1$ with $\delta(e_i)=x_i$ and $\delta(R)=0$; thus $\delta(ab)=\delta(a)b+(-1)^pa\delta(b)$ for homogeneous $a$ of degree $p$.

The **Koszul complex with coefficients in $M$** is $K(\mathbf x;M)=(\bigwedge R^n\otimes_R M,d)$, where $d=\delta\otimes\operatorname{id}_M$. Its degree-$p$ term is $\bigwedge^pR^n\otimes_R M$ for $0\leq p\leq n$, and zero otherwise. Explicitly,

$$d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes m)=\sum_{j=1}^p(-1)^{j-1}e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_j}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}\otimes x_{i_j}m.$$

The empty wedge is $1\in R$. In particular $d(e_i\otimes m)=1\otimes x_im$ in $K_0=R\otimes_R M$, canonically identified with $M$ by $r\otimes m\mapsto rm$ with inverse $m\mapsto1\otimes m$. The differential out of degree zero is zero. The derivation respects the exterior relations and the two orders of deleting distinct factors cancel in $d^2$, so these maps form a chain complex. For $n=0$ this is $M$ in degree zero under the same identification.
If $M$ is finite free and $\mathbf x$ is $M$-regular, then $K(\mathbf x;M)$ is a finite free resolution of $M/(\mathbf x)M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be Noetherian local, let $0\ne M$ be finite, and let
$x_1,\ldots,x_r$ be both $M$-regular and an initial segment of a system of
parameters for $M$. Then $M$ is Cohen--Macaulay if and only if
$M/(x_1,\ldots,x_r)M$ is Cohen--Macaulay.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$ is a domain and Cohen–Macaulay. For every regular system $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, the tuple is $R$-regular and $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is regular local of dimension $d-c$ for all $0\le c\le d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $R$ is a Noetherian Cohen--Macaulay ring, then
$R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$ is Cohen--Macaulay for every $n\ge0$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\alpha$ be a root of a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra
$\mathfrak g$ with respect to a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, with coroot
$h_\alpha$ as in [[def-coroot-of-a-lie-algebra-root]]. Then there are
$e_\alpha\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$ and $f_\alpha\in\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$ with

$$[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=h_\alpha,\qquad [h_\alpha,e_\alpha]=2e_\alpha,\qquad [h_\alpha,f_\alpha]=-2f_\alpha .$$

Consequently the span of $e_\alpha,f_\alpha,h_\alpha$ is a copy of
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ inside $\mathfrak g$
([[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]]).

Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple
Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex
semisimple Lie algebra, let $\mathfrak h$ be a Cartan subalgebra, and let
$\Phi=\Phi(\mathfrak g,\mathfrak h)$ be the set of roots of
[[def-root-and-root-space-relative-to-a-cartan-subalgebra]]. Then $\Phi$ is
finite and
$$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha$$
is a direct sum of $\mathfrak h$ with the nonzero root spaces.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra, and let $B$ be its Killing form from [[def-killing-form-of-a-semisimple-lie-algebra]]. Then

$$B([x,y],z)=B(x,[y,z]) \qquad (x,y,z\in \mathfrak g),$$

and $B$ is nondegenerate.

For a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ in
characteristic zero,
$\operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak g)=\operatorname{ad}(\mathfrak g)$.
The representing element is unique because $Z(\mathfrak g)=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $G$ be an affine group scheme of finite type over $k$ ([[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]). Then the structure morphism $G\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth, that is, $G$ is a smooth group scheme over $k$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]). In particular every local ring $\mathcal O_{G,g}$ is regular and $G$ is reduced. No smoothness, reducedness or finiteness of $G$ beyond finite type is assumed, and the characteristic-zero hypothesis is essential: in characteristic $p>0$ the finite group schemes $\alpha_p$ and $\mu_p$ are not smooth.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field and let $G$ be a connected affine group variety over $k$, i.e. a smooth connected affine algebraic group of finite type over $k$ ([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]], [[def-group-scheme-over-a-field]]). Then: (a) for every Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G$ the quotient $G/B$ is complete; (b) any two Borel subgroups of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (c) any two maximal tori of $G$ are conjugate by an element of $G(k)$; (d) any two Borel pairs are conjugate. The assertions here are made under the stated smooth connected and algebraically closed hypotheses; no necessity claim for each hypothesis is made.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field, let
$X$ and $Y$ be $k$-schemes that are locally standard smooth over $k$ at the
points considered below ([[def-ag-standard-smooth-algebra]]), and let
$f\colon X\to Y$ be a morphism of $k$-schemes of finite type
([[def-locally-finite-type-and-finite-type-morphism]]). Let $x\in X$ be a
$k$-rational point and put $y=f(x)$, assumed $k$-rational as well, so that
$\kappa(x)=\kappa(y)=k$ ([[def-residue-field-scheme-point]]). Write
$A=\mathcal O_{Y,y}$, $S=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, with maximal ideals
$\mathfrak m_y\subseteq A$, $\mathfrak m_x\subseteq S$, and let
$f^{*}\colon A\to S$ be the induced local homomorphism. Let
$X_y=X\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ be the scheme-theoretic fibre
([[def-scheme-theoretic-fibre]]), whose local ring at $x$ is
$S/\mathfrak m_yS$. Then:

1. **Submersion criterion.** $f$ is locally standard smooth at $x$ — that is,
   there are affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}C\subseteq X$ and
   $\operatorname{Spec}D\subseteq Y$ with $x\in\operatorname{Spec}C$,
   $f(\operatorname{Spec}C)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}D$ and $D\to C$ standard
   smooth at the prime of $C$ corresponding to $x$ — if and only if the
   $k$-linear map
   $f^{*}\colon\mathfrak m_y/\mathfrak m_y^{2}\to\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^{2}$
   induced by $f^{*}$ is injective.
2. **Flatness and fibres.** If the equivalent conditions of clause 1 hold and
   $m=\dim S$, $n=\dim A$, then $S$ is flat over $A$, that is $f$ is flat at
   $x$, and $S/\mathfrak m_yS$ is a regular local ring of dimension $m-n$; in
   other words the fibre $X_y$ is regular at $x$ of dimension $m-n$. Any
   standard smooth chart of $f$ at $x$ has relative dimension $m-n$.

The two schemes are only required to be locally standard smooth at $x$ and $y$,
not globally; $f$ is of finite type as assumed above, and no hypothesis is
imposed on the base field. The Axiom of Choice is used
through the local-flatness, regular-parameter and geometric-regularity
suppliers cited below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $R\to B$ be a finitely presented ring
map ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]). Then the set of primes
$\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B$ at which $B_{\mathfrak q}$ is flat over $R$
is open in $\operatorname{Spec}B$. The same statement holds with a finitely
presented $B$-module $M$ in place of $B$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $f:X\to S$ be a morphism of schemes that
is flat ([[def-flat-morphism-schemes]]) and locally of finite presentation
([[def-locally-finite-presentation-morphism]]). Then $f$ is universally open
([[def-open-morphism-schemes]]); in particular $f$ is open. No further
hypothesis is imposed on $X$, $S$ or $f$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be an
algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, let $X$ and $Y$ be
irreducible classical varieties over $k$, and let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a
dominant morphism. Regard $X$ and $Y$ as integral finite-type $k$-schemes
under
[[thm-classical-varieties-equivalent-integral-separated-finite-type-schemes]],
let $X_{\mathrm{reg}},Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ be their regular loci
([[def-singular-and-regular-loci-variety]]), and let
$$U=X_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap f^{-1}(Y_{\mathrm{reg}})\cap D(H)$$
be the nonempty open subset of $X$ produced by
[[lem-dominant-map-generic-differential-surjectivity-char-zero]], so that
$f(U)\subseteq Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $d_xf$ is surjective at every closed point
$x\in U$.

Then there are a nonempty affine open subvariety
$V\subseteq U$ of $X$ — explicitly a nonempty principal open $D_{X_0}(h')$ of
an affine chart $X_0$ of $X$ — and a nonempty affine open subvariety
$W\subseteq Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$ — a nonempty principal open of an affine chart
of $Y$ — such that:

1. $f(V)\subseteq W$, and $V\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and
   $W\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ are smooth, so that $V$ and $W$ are smooth
   affine classical varieties over $k$;
2. the restriction $f|_V\colon V\to W$ is a morphism of finite type and is
   smooth in the sense of [[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]: it is locally
   standard smooth at every point of $V$; consequently the restriction
   $f|_V\colon V\to Y$ (equivalently $V\to Y_{\mathrm{reg}}$) is smooth as
   well.

In particular $f$ is smooth at every point of the nonempty open subset $V$ of
its source. Neither $X$ nor $Y$ is assumed smooth outside its regular locus,
and the target-side statement — a dense open subset of $Y$ over which the
source is smooth — is *not* asserted here: it requires a smooth source and
fails without that hypothesis.

For an irreducible classical variety $X$ and morphism $f:X\to Y$, the reduced closure $Z=\overline{f(X)}$ is irreducible and $\dim X=\dim Z+r$, where $r$ is the common dimension of the nonempty fibres on a nonempty open of $Z$. For arbitrary nonempty $X$ with components $X_i$, $\dim X=\max_i(\dim\overline{f(X_i)}+r_i)$, with a separately chosen generic open and relative dimension $r_i$ for each $X_i$. For empty $X$ use the empty maximum $-\infty$.

Work over a fixed algebraically closed field $k$, with the Axiom of Choice. Classical varieties are separated and admit finite affine covers; they may be reducible or empty unless irreducibility is specified. Irreducible means nonempty. All fibres and points below are classical closed-point fibres and points.

Let $k$ be a field, let $n\geq 0$ be finite, put $P=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and let
$A=P/I$ with a specified finite generating list $I=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)$ for the
actual ideal defining the affine scheme. For a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset
A$, write $L=A/\mathfrak m$. Let $J(\mathfrak m)$ be the $r\times n$ matrix over
$L$ obtained by mapping the formal partial derivatives $\partial f_i/\partial
t_j$ through $P\to A\to L$.

If $k$ is perfect, then $L/k$ is finite separable and
$$
\operatorname{rank}_L J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}
$$
if and only if $A_{\mathfrak m}$ is a regular local ring. For any field $k$,
the same equivalence holds at a $k$-rational point, where $L=k$, without a
perfectness assumption. If $I=I(X)$ for a reduced classical affine algebraic
set $X$ over an algebraically closed field and $\mathfrak m$ corresponds to a
closed point $x$, then, assuming AC,
$$
\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim_xX=\max_{x\in X_i}\dim X_i,
$$
where $X_i$ ranges over the irreducible components through $x$. The finite
generating list need not be minimal, and $I$ need not be radical in the first
two assertions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A regular local ring $R$ of dimension $d$ is a domain and Cohen–Macaulay. For every regular system $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, the tuple is $R$-regular and $R/(x_1,\ldots,x_c)$ is regular local of dimension $d-c$ for all $0\le c\le d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring.
The natural map
$$R\longrightarrow\prod_{\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(R)}R_{\mathfrak q}$$
is injective. For each $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(R)$,
the local ring $R_{\mathfrak q}$ has a nonzero element
annihilated by its maximal ideal $\mathfrak qR_{\mathfrak q}$;
in particular it has depth zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, the enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak g)$ is a free left, hence also right, module over its center $Z(U(\mathfrak g))$.

derivations.claim: If $\mathfrak g=0$ then $r=0$, $A=\mathbb C$ and all assertions are immediate; hence assume $\mathfrak g\ne0$. The images of $p_1,\dots,p_r$ generate the ideal $S(\mathfrak g)\,S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}_+$, the sequence is regular by [F2], and the Koszul Euler characteristic gives $\operatorname{Hilb}(A,t)=\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$; as a polynomial this has degree $\sum_i(d_i-1)=\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N$ and leading coefficient $1$, so $\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r$ and $A$ is Cohen-Macaulay at every maximal ideal by [F2].

Choose for every simple root $\alpha_i$ an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple $(e_i,f_i,h_i)$ and put $e=\sum_ie_i$, $h=2\rho^\vee=\sum_ih_i$, $f=\sum_if_i$; then $[h,e]=2e$, $[h,f]=-2f$ and $[e,f]=h$. Complete reducibility writes the adjoint module as a direct sum of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-strings $L(2m_1)\oplus\cdots$; each string contributes exactly one vector killed by $h$, and $\ker\operatorname{ad}h=\mathfrak h$ has dimension $r$, so there are exactly $r$ strings; a string with $m_j=0$ would consist of a nonzero vector killed by $e$ and $h$, i.e. a nonzero element of $\mathfrak h$ commuting with all $e_i$, which is central in $\mathfrak g$, hence zero; so all $m_j\ge1$ and counting dimensions gives $\sum_j(2m_j+1)=\dim\mathfrak g=2N+r$, that is $\sum_jm_j=N$. The highest vector of a string has $\operatorname{ad}h$-eigenvalue $2m_j>0$, hence lies in $\mathfrak n^+=\bigoplus_{\alpha>0}\mathfrak g_\alpha$; therefore $\ker\operatorname{ad}e$ is the $r$-dimensional span of the highest vectors and lies in $\mathfrak n^+$, and the lowest vectors span $z_f:=\ker\operatorname{ad}f\subseteq\mathfrak n^-$ with $\mathfrak g=[\mathfrak g,e]\oplus z_f$.

Let $\varphi_t(x)=t\cdot\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})(x)$ for $t\in\mathbb C^\times$. Since $p_i$ is $\mathfrak g$-invariant, $p_i(\varphi_tx)=t^{d_i}p_i(x)$ for all $x\in\mathfrak g$; since $\operatorname{Ad}(t^{-\rho^\vee})f_i=tf_i$, the map $\varphi_t$ preserves $z_f$, so with $q_i(y):=p_i(e+y)$ one has $q_i(\varphi_ty)=p_i(\varphi_t(e+y))=t^{d_i}q_i(y)$: each $q_i$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $d_i$ for the weights $\deg y_j=m_j+1$ on $z_f$; indeed a root vector of height $t$ has $\varphi$-weight $1-t$, so the lowest vector $y_j$ has weight $m_j+1\ge2$.

Let $G=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathfrak g)^0$ and let $N_+=\exp(\operatorname{ad}\mathfrak n^+)$, $H$ the torus of root characters; both are closed connected subgroups and $B=H\cdot N_+\subseteq G$ is a Borel subgroup with Lie algebra $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$: its Lie algebra is solvable, and any solvable subalgebra containing a negative root vector together with its root $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ would contain a copy of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, so $\mathfrak b$ is maximal solvable. By [F4], $G$ is a smooth irreducible affine algebraic group of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g$ acting morphically on $\mathfrak g$, and all its Borel subgroups are conjugate.

The morphism $\Psi:G\times z_f\to\mathfrak g$, $(g,y)\mapsto g\cdot(e+y)$, is dominant. Its differential at $(1,0)$ is $(\xi,y)\mapsto[\xi,e]+y$ for $\xi\in T_1G=\mathfrak g$ (using $G$-equivariance of the action), with image $[\mathfrak g,e]+z_f=\mathfrak g$ by step 1.2; hence the cotangent map is injective and, by the submersion criterion at the rational points $(1,0)$ and $e$, $\Psi$ is locally standard smooth, hence flat, at $(1,0)$; the flat locus is open and flat morphisms of finite presentation are open, so the image of $\Psi$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathfrak g$; since $\mathfrak g$ is irreducible, $\Psi$ is dominant.

Every nilpotent element $x\in\mathfrak g$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$: the element $u=\exp(\operatorname{ad}x)\in G$ is unipotent, so it lies in some Borel subgroup, which is conjugate to $B$; hence $y:=g\cdot x$ satisfies $\exp(\operatorname{ad}y)\in B$, and the logarithm, inverse to the exponential on the unipotent radical, gives $\operatorname{ad}y\in\mathfrak n^+$; since $\operatorname{ad}$ is injective, $y\in\mathfrak n^+$. Conversely, $p_i$ vanishes on $\mathfrak n^+$: for $n\in\mathfrak n^+$ one has $\operatorname{Ad}(t^{\rho^\vee})n\to0$ as $t\to0$, while $p_i(n)=p_i(\operatorname{Ad}(t^{\rho^\vee})n)$ for all $t$ by invariance, so continuity gives $p_i(n)=p_i(0)=0$.

The central reduction has associated graded $A$: fix a central character $\chi:Z\to\mathbb C$ with kernel $\mathfrak m_\chi$, and let $J=\mathfrak m_\chi U(\mathfrak g)$. By [F6], $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)=S(\mathfrak g)$, $\operatorname{gr}Z=S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}$, and the leading symbol of any $z\in\mathfrak m_\chi$ lies in $S(\mathfrak g)^{\mathfrak g}_+=(p_1,\dots,p_r)$; conversely each $p_i$ is the leading symbol of an element of $\mathfrak m_\chi$, for instance of $z_i-\chi(z_i)$ for a central element $z_i$ of leading symbol $p_i$ (the scalar term has lower filtration degree because $d_i>0$). Therefore $\operatorname{gr}J=(p_1,\dots,p_r)S(\mathfrak g)$ and the natural graded surjection $S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{gr}(U(\mathfrak g)/J)$ is an isomorphism: both sides have the Hilbert series of step 1.1, since the filtered free harmonic decomposition of [F6] restricts to a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)/J$ whose symbols have exactly the Hilbert series $\prod_i(1-t^{d_i})/(1-t)^{\dim\mathfrak g}$. Hence the PBW associated graded of $U(\mathfrak g)/U(\mathfrak g)\ker\chi$ is canonically $A$.

The restrictions $q_1,\dots,q_r\in\mathbb C[z_f]$ are algebraically independent: the pullback $\Psi^*$ is injective because $\Psi$ is dominant, and $\Psi^*(p_i)=q_i$ by $G$-invariance of the $p_i$; if a nonzero polynomial $F$ satisfied $F(q_1,\dots,q_r)=0$, then $\Psi^*(F(p_1,\dots,p_r))=0$, hence $F(p_1,\dots,p_r)=0$ in $S(\mathfrak g)$, contradicting the algebraic independence of $p_1,\dots,p_r$ from [F1].

The common zero set $\mathcal N=\{x:p_i(x)=0\text{ for all }i\}$ equals $G\cdot\mathfrak n^+$: the inclusion $\supseteq$ is step 2.2, and conversely if all $p_i$ vanish then every invariant polynomial of positive degree vanishes, so the invariant traces $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{ad}x)^k)$, $k\ge1$, vanish because each is invariant with zero constant term; Newton's identities express every coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of $\operatorname{ad}x$ polynomially in these traces, so the characteristic polynomial is $T^{\dim\mathfrak g}$, hence $\operatorname{ad}x$ is nilpotent and $x$ is conjugate into $\mathfrak n^+$ by step 2.2. Also $\mathcal N$ is the underlying set of $\operatorname{Spec}A$.

The map $q=(q_1,\dots,q_r):\mathbb A^r\to\mathbb A^r$ is dominant by step 3.1, and $\mathbb A^r$ is smooth, so generic smoothness provides a dense open subset of $\mathbb A^r$ on which the differential of $q$ is surjective; in particular the Jacobian determinant $D=\det(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)$ is not identically zero.

Weights: $D$ is weighted-homogeneous of weighted degree $\sum_id_i-\sum_j(m_j+1)=\sum_i(d_i-1)-\sum_jm_j=N-N=0$ by steps 1.2 and 1.3, because the derivative with respect to $y_j$ lowers weighted degree by $m_j+1$; a nonzero polynomial all of whose monomials have positive weights $m_j+1$ and total weighted degree zero is a nonzero constant. Hence $D$ is a nonzero constant, and in particular the linear map $z_f\to\mathbb C^r$, $y\mapsto(dp_1(e)(y),\dots,dp_r(e)(y))$, given by the matrix $(\partial q_i/\partial y_j)(0)$, is invertible.

The Jacobian matrix of the presentation $A=S(\mathfrak g)/(p_1,\dots,p_r)$ at the rational maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $e$ has rank exactly $r$: its rows are the differentials $dp_i(e)$, which are linearly independent by step 5.1. Since $\dim A_{\mathfrak m}=\dim A=\dim\mathfrak g-r$ by step 1.1, the Jacobian criterion in the form $\operatorname{rank}J(\mathfrak m)=n-\dim A_{\mathfrak m}$ identifies $A_{\mathfrak m}$ as a regular local ring.

Regularity propagates along the orbit and is generic: for $g\in G$ the induced automorphism of $A$ carries the local ring at $e$ to the local ring at $g\cdot e$, so $A$ is regular at every point of the orbit $G\cdot e$; that orbit has dimension $\dim G-\dim\operatorname{Stab}_G(e)=\dim\mathfrak g-r$ because $\operatorname{Lie}\operatorname{Stab}_G(e)=\operatorname{ad}(\ker\operatorname{ad}e)$ has dimension $r$ by step 1.2. The orbit is contained in $\mathcal N$, which is irreducible as the image of the irreducible variety $G\times\mathfrak n^+$ under the action morphism; hence $G\cdot e$ is dense in $\operatorname{Spec}A$. Therefore the regular locus of $A$, which is a nonempty open subset, contains the generic point of the irreducible space $\operatorname{Spec}A$.

Consequences: $A$ is Cohen-Macaulay by step 1.1, so by [F5] every associated prime of $A$ is minimal; since the underlying topological space $\operatorname{Spec}A=\mathcal N$ is irreducible by step 7.1, there is exactly one minimal prime $\mathfrak p_0$, and $\{\mathfrak p_0\}=\operatorname{Ass}(A)$. By step 7.1 the localization $A_{\mathfrak p_0}$ is a regular local ring of dimension zero, hence a field; the injection $A\to\prod_{\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Ass}(A)}A_{\mathfrak q}=A_{\mathfrak p_0}$ of [F5] is therefore a ring map into a field, so $A$ is reduced; being reduced with a single minimal prime, $A$ is a domain.

Combining steps 1.1, 2.3, 8.1: $A$ is a reduced integral domain of dimension $\dim\mathfrak g-r=2N=2|\Phi^+|$ with the displayed Hilbert series, and every central reduction has associated graded $A$. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory, group-theoretic and geometric suppliers [F1], [F4], [F5] and [F6]; the conclusions themselves are choice-free statements about $\mathfrak g$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ act on the Cartan space $\mathfrak h$ by reflections and on
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ by graded algebra automorphisms, with coinvariant algebra
$C=S/I$ as in [[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]. Then there
is a $W$-stable graded subspace $\mathcal H\subseteq S$, finite dimensional of
dimension $|W|$, such that the multiplication map
$$S^W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S,\qquad p\otimes h\mapsto ph,$$
is an isomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules, and the
restriction of the quotient map $\rho:S\to C$ to $\mathcal H$ is an isomorphism
of graded $W$-modules $\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }C$. One may take
$$\mathcal H=\{f\in S:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\},$$
the kernel of the $W$-equivariant Laplacian attached to a $W$-invariant
positive definite form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$, or any $W$-stable graded
complement of $I$. In particular $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$ and
$\sum_d\dim\mathcal H_d=|W|$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group acting faithfully on its $r$-dimensional complex reflection representation $V$, and put $S=\mathbb C[V]$. Then $S^W$ is a polynomial algebra on $r$ homogeneous algebraically independent basic invariants, and $S$ is free of rank $|W|$ over $S^W$. More generally these conclusions hold for every finite subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ generated by complex reflections (nonidentity transformations fixing a hyperplane pointwise). In the Weyl case the generating root reflections have order two; no classification or Coxeter presentation is needed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $W\leq\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite complex reflection group, in particular a finite Weyl reflection group, with $r=\dim V$. Put $S=\mathbb C[V]$, $R=S^W$, $I=SR_+$, and let $d_1,\ldots,d_r$ be the degrees of basic invariants. Then
$$\operatorname{Hilb}(S/I,t)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+t+\cdots+t^{d_i-1}),\qquad \dim_{\mathbb C}(S/I)=\prod_i d_i=|W|.$$

Let $G$ be a finite group. The irreducible complex characters of $G$,
$\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$, form an orthonormal basis of the complex vector space
$\mathrm{cf}(G)$ of class functions on $G$, with respect to the standard
inner product.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]) and let $G$ be a group. A
**finite-dimensional representation of $G$ over $k$** is a finite-dimensional
$k$-vector space $V$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-dimension]]) together with a
group homomorphism
$$\rho:G\longrightarrow \operatorname{GL}(V),$$
where $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ denotes the group of invertible $k$-linear maps
$V \to V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]], [[def-group-homomorphism]]).

The associated action is
$$g \cdot v:=\rho(g)(v).$$
This makes $V$ into a $G$-module over $k$ in the sense of
[[def-g-module-over-a-commutative-ring]].

The **degree** of the representation is the dimension of its underlying vector
space:
$$\deg(\rho):=\dim_k V.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\sim}C$ is an isomorphism of graded $W$-modules, so the graded traces agree: $\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)=\operatorname{HTr}(\mathcal H,t)(w)$ for every $w\in W$.

Molien's formula for the graded trace of $S$: for $|t|<1$ and $w\in W$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r$ on $\mathfrak h^*$, one has $\operatorname{tr}(w\mid S_i)=h_i(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_r)$, the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial of degree $i$, whose generating function is $\sum_{i\ge0}h_i(\lambda)t^i=\prod_j(1-t\lambda_j)^{-1}$; with page degrees doubled this gives $\operatorname{HTr}(S,t)(w)=\det(1-t^2w\mid\mathfrak h^*)^{-1}$ as an identity of formal power series, the finite sum over the eigenvalues making every coefficient finite.

Since $S\cong S^W\otimes\mathcal H$ with $W$ acting trivially on the polynomial ring $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$, whose homogeneous piece of page degree $2D$ has dimension equal to the number of monomials of weighted degree $D$, the graded trace factors as $\operatorname{HTr}(S,t)(w)=\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})^{-1}\cdot\operatorname{HTr}(\mathcal H,t)(w)$ for $|t|<1$.

Combining steps 1.1 to 1.3, $$\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\operatorname{HTr}(S,t)(w)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1-t^{2d_i})\cdot\det(1-t^2w\mid\mathfrak h^*)^{-1},$$ first as an identity of formal power series for $|t|<1$ and then as an identity of rational functions; this is assertion (2).

Limits at $t	o1$: each factor $1-t^{2d_i}$ vanishes to order exactly one at $t=1$ because its derivative there is $-2d_i
eq0$, so the numerator vanishes to order $r$. The denominator $\det(1-t^2w\mid\mathfrak h^*)=\prod_j(1-t^2\lambda_j)$ vanishes at $t=1$ to the order of the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $1$ of $w$ on $\mathfrak h^*$, that is, to order $\dim\mathfrak h^w$; the reflection representation is faithful, so $w
eq1$ implies $\mathfrak h^w
eq\mathfrak h$ and $\dim\mathfrak h^w\le r-1$, whence for $w
eq1$ the limit of $\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)$ is $0$. At $w=1$ the quotient is $\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})/(1-t^2)^r	o\prod_id_i=|W|$ by [F2].

The graded trace at $t=1$ is the ordinary character of the finite-dimensional $W$-module $C$, so step 3.1 shows $\chi_C(w)=|W|\delta_{w,1}$, the character of the regular representation; by the orthonormality of irreducible characters [F3], the multiplicity of each irreducible $E$ in $C$ equals its multiplicity in $\mathbb C W$, namely $\dim E$. Hence $C\cong\mathbb C W$ as $W$-modules, which is assertion (1).

Graded multiplicities: the decomposition of $C$ into isotypic components is multiplicity-free with respect to the grading in the sense that each irreducible $E$ occurs in a uniquely determined graded multiplicity series $\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)$, and the identities $\sum_E\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)\chi_E(w)=\operatorname{HTr}(C,t)(w)$ for all $w$ determine $\operatorname{mult}_E(C,t)$ as the coefficient of $\chi_E$ in the expansion of the graded character in the orthonormal basis of [F3]; setting $t=1$ recovers $\operatorname{mult}_E(C,1)$ as the multiplicity of $E$ in $C$, which is $\dim E$ by step 4.1; this is assertion (3). The Hilbert-series specialization of step 2.1 at $w=1$ is $\prod_i(1-t^{2d_i})/(1-t^2)^r=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)})$.

Multiplication gives a vector-space isomorphism

$$U(\mathfrak n^-)\xrightarrow{\sim}M(\lambda),\qquad u\longmapsto uv_\lambda.$$

Consequently, ordered negative-root PBW monomials from
[[thm-pbw-ordered-monomial-basis-for-the-enveloping-algebra]] applied to
$v_\lambda$ form a basis.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_r$ be an ordered basis of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Then the monomials

$$x_1^{a_1}x_2^{a_2}\cdots x_r^{a_r} \qquad (a_i\in \mathbb N_0)$$

form a basis of $U(\mathfrak g)$. In particular, multiplication identifies $\operatorname{gr}U(\mathfrak g)$ with the symmetric algebra $S(\mathfrak g)$ on the symbols of the $x_i$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

Every object of $\mathcal O$ has a finite composition series and is both Noetherian and Artinian. The length of zero is zero.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

The simple objects of $\mathcal O$ are exactly the modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, and $L(\lambda)\cong L(\mu)$ if and only if $\lambda=\mu$. Simplicity here excludes zero.
Every nonzero $\mathfrak g$-homomorphism $M(\mu)\to M(\lambda)$ is injective.

For a $\mathfrak g$-module $V$, sending a homomorphism $T:M(\lambda)\to V$
to $T(v_\lambda)$ is a bijection onto the vectors $v\in V$ of weight
$\lambda$ annihilated by $\mathfrak n^+$.  Here $M(\lambda)$ is
[[def-verma-module]].  The nonzero vectors in this target are precisely the
highest-weight vectors of weight $\lambda$ from
[[def-highest-weight-vector-and-cyclic-highest-weight-module]]; the zero vector
corresponds to the zero homomorphism.

There is a unique Chevalley-contravariant bilinear form $S_\lambda$ on
$M(\lambda)$ with $S_\lambda(v_\lambda,v_\lambda)=1$.

The radical of $S_\lambda$ is $J(\lambda)$, the unique maximal submodule.
Thus $S_\lambda$ descends to a nondegenerate form on $L(\lambda)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Fix a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$, and a positive Borel $\mathfrak b=\mathfrak h\oplus\mathfrak n^+$. Write $Q^+=\sum_i\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\alpha_i$, $\mu\leq\lambda$ when $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$, and $w\cdot\lambda=w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$.

Restricted Chevalley duality is an exact contravariant equivalence $D:\mathcal O\to\mathcal O^{\mathrm{op}}$, with a natural isomorphism $D^2\cong\operatorname{id}$. It preserves each weight-space dimension, the formal character, and every simple composition multiplicity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $E$ be a
finite-dimensional $\mathfrak h$-semisimple $\mathfrak g$-module with weight
multiplicities $\dim E_\eta$
([[def-weight-and-weight-space-of-a-lie-algebra-representation]]). For every
weight $\mu$, the object $E\otimes\Delta(\mu)$ has a finite Verma flag
([[def-verma-flag-and-its-multiplicities]]) whose factors are $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$,
the factor $\Delta(\mu+\eta)$ occurring $\dim E_\eta$ times; the factors can be

Consequently, if $X\in\mathcal O$ has a finite Verma flag with multiplicities

$$(E\otimes X:\Delta(\mu))=\sum_\eta\dim E_\eta\,(X:\Delta(\mu-\eta)).$$
